ob_01: Objection handling. This is not a list of clever comebacks — memorized rebuttals make you sound like you are selling, and they collapse the moment a firm says something you did not rehearse. What you are learning here is a repeatable structure you can run on any objection, even one you have never heard. The goal is judgment, not a script.
ob_02: The structure — six steps. One, acknowledge the concern; never argue. Two, identify what they are actually protecting. Three, clarify the real workflow. Four, state one three seven's narrow role. Five, ask a diagnostic question. Six, decide whether to keep going or to disqualify honestly. Every objection ahead follows this same shape.
ob_03: When they say we already have intake software, they usually mean I do not want another disconnected system. Do not attack the tool they use. Acknowledge it, then place us before it — one three seven organizes the worker's underlying record before your team has to reconstruct it, and it feeds the system you already have. Then ask what their staff still assembles by hand before an attorney can screen.
ob_04: We already use A I often means we have seen the hype and we are skeptical. Agree with the skepticism. Say we use A I too — the difference is what we let it do: we organize and link to the source, and we never let it judge the case. Then ask which part of intake their current A I actually touches. Usually it is drafting, not the worker's raw record.
ob_05: Workers will not upload everything is a real concern, not a brush-off. What they are protecting is staff time wasted on incomplete files. Say the worker owns the record and is motivated — it is their claim — and the system shows them exactly what is missing and even writes the request letter. Then ask what share of their current intakes arrive complete on the first pass.
ob_06: Our staff already handles this means do not threaten my people. Never frame this as replacing staff. Say we hand your staff the reconstructed file so they spend their time on judgment, not on assembly. Then ask how many hours a week that assembly currently takes across the team. The number is usually bigger than they expect once they add it up.
ob_07: We do not have enough volume can be a genuine disqualifier — respect it. What they may mean is I am not sure this pays off. Say the value is per-intake time saved and cleaner screening, not raw volume. Then ask how many potential matters they turn away or leave half-built each month. And if the honest answer is that they are not a fit yet, say so — that builds more trust than a forced pitch.
ob_08: We cannot trust A I with legal intake — good, they should not blindly. What they are protecting is their bar license and their liability under California A B three-sixteen, which says the lawyer cannot blame the tool. Say that is exactly why every fact links to its source page — nothing is taken on faith, everything is one click to verify. Then ask what it would take for them to trust an automated file. The answer is almost always traceability, which is our entire design.
ob_09: We do not want another tool means tool fatigue. Do not oversell an integration you cannot yet prove. Say one three seven sits before or beside what they already use — the worker does the work, and the firm simply receives a finished file. Then ask what happens today between a worker first reaching out and the moment an attorney can actually make a decision.
ob_10: How is this different from a chatbot or a document-summary product — treat this as your opening, not a threat. Say a chatbot answers questions and a summarizer condenses documents, but one three seven builds the worker's own source-linked record and hands them ownership of it. Different job, earlier in the timeline. Then ask whether their current tools produce anything the worker actually keeps and controls.
ob_11: This is the dangerous one — can it tell us whether the worker has a case. This is the objection most likely to tempt you across the doctrine line. The wrong answer sounds helpful — something like, our A I finds the strong cases before your team touches them. Never say that. It is untrue to what we do, and it puts both of us at legal risk.
ob_12: Here is the line you hold instead. Say it clearly: no, and that is deliberate. We organize and reflect the record; your firm makes every legal and screening decision. We show what is present and what is missing against what the law requires — we never conclude whether there is a claim. Then turn it into a question: would a complete, source-linked record make your own screening decision faster? Hold that line with confidence — it is what keeps us clean and what keeps them safe.
ob_13: That is the set. Notice that none of these were comebacks — each one acknowledged the concern, clarified the workflow, stated our narrow role, and ended in a question. Run the structure, not a memorized line. And whenever you are unsure, fall back to the one move that is always safe: describe the record, and let the attorney decide.
